Topic pages apply criminological mechanisms, institutional analysis, and models to substantive crime areas. They are not meant to be isolated summaries. Each topic should connect crime type, mechanism, measurement, evidence, and policy.

The goal is to ask: what kind of behaviour is being studied, why does it occur, how is it measured, and what does intervention change?

Each topic can involve several mechanisms at once. For example, drug markets may involve demand, addiction, organized distribution, enforcement displacement, violence, and institutional mistrust.

## Topic-page template

Each topic should ideally follow this structure:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[Define the crime type] --> B[Identify main behaviours]
    B --> C[Identify mechanisms]
    C --> D[Discuss measurement problems]
    D --> E[Connect to institutions]
    E --> F[Use simple models]
    F --> G[Evaluate policy trade-offs]
```

This prevents topic pages from becoming mere lists of facts. The focus should remain analytical.

## Comparing topic areas

| Topic | Central mechanisms | Major measurement issue |
|---|---|---|
| Violent crime | conflict, retaliation, emotion, peer norms, weapons | underreporting and seriousness variation |
| Property crime | opportunity, target suitability, guardianship | reporting depends on insurance, value, and trust |
| Organized crime | illicit governance, reputation, corruption, violence | hidden structure and weak observability |
| White-collar crime | agency problems, compliance failure, regulatory gaps | detection depends on audit and investigation |
| Cybercrime | anonymity, automation, social engineering, platforms | cross-border attribution and underreporting |
| Drug markets | demand, addiction, enforcement pressure, substitution | hidden transactions and enforcement bias |

This table is only a starting point. Each crime area contains internal diversity.

## From topic to mechanism

A substantive topic is not yet an explanation. To explain a crime pattern, we need a mechanism.

For example:

```text
property crime
→ opportunity and weak guardianship
→ target selection
→ spatial concentration
```

or:

```text
violent crime
→ conflict plus peer audience
→ status threat
→ retaliation
```

or:

```text
white-collar crime
→ agency problem plus weak monitoring
→ rule violation
→ delayed detection
```

The move from topic to mechanism is the move from description to explanation.

## From topic to model

Topic pages also connect to models.

| Topic | Possible model |
|---|---|
| Violent crime | repeated conflict or retaliation game |
| Property crime | target-selection or inspection game |
| Organized crime | repeated enforcement and reputation model |
| White-collar crime | principal-agent or audit game |
| Cybercrime | attacker-defender game |
| Drug markets | illicit market equilibrium or network model |

The model should be chosen because it clarifies a mechanism.

## Policy comparison

Different topics create different policy problems.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Crime topic] --> B[Mechanism]
    B --> C[Institutional response]
    C --> D[Behavioural adaptation]
    D --> E[Policy outcome]
    E --> F[Unintended effects]
```

For example, enforcement against drug markets may reduce visible dealing in one place while shifting activity elsewhere. Cybercrime enforcement may remove one platform while offenders migrate to another. White-collar regulation may reduce some misconduct while creating compliance theatre.

## Common mistakes

### 1. Treating a topic as a mechanism

“Cybercrime” is not a mechanism. It is a domain. The mechanism may be anonymity, automation, deception, or weak enforcement.

### 2. Treating official data as complete

Many topic areas are heavily underreported or dependent on detection.

### 3. Assuming one policy fits all crime types

Violent crime, cybercrime, fraud, and drug markets respond to different mechanisms.

### 4. Ignoring adaptation

Offenders, institutions, and markets adapt to interventions.

### 5. Ignoring harm variation

The same legal category may contain events with very different harms.
